strengths: Well-motivated approach with a clear motivational study (Section 2.2, Figures 3, 9-11) that convincingly demonstrates the shortcomings of existing T2I-based editing (NTI, MCPL) for counterfactual generation, including prompt sensitivity and lack of fine-grained numeric control—this grounds the method's design choices empirically rather than by assertion.

The proposed Causal-Adapter is a modular, lightweight design that keeps the diffusion backbone frozen, making the method computationally practical (single A100 GPU, training within a day) and easily transferable across the causal graph/attribute set by only swapping the small causal-mechanism module and adapter.

Comprehensive experiments spanning three distinct domains (synthetic Pendulum, human faces CelebA, medical MRI ADNI) with four complementary evaluation axes (effectiveness, composition, realism, minimality) and consistent, often large, improvements over strong baselines (VAE, HVAE, GAN, CausalVAE, DisDiffAE, CausalDiffAE).

Thorough ablation studies isolating the contributions of PAI and CTC regularizers, both quantitatively (Figure 8, Tables 6-9) and qualitatively via cross-attention visualizations (Figure 3c, Figure 16), providing good mechanistic insight into why the regularizers help (semantic-spatial alignment and token disentanglement).

Extensive supplementary material (extended ablations on guidance scale, DDIM steps, attention guidance; additional qualitative results across all three datasets; attention map visualizations) substantially strengthens reproducibility and supports the paper's claims beyond the main text.

Honest and specific limitations discussion (Appendix F) identifying a genuine failure mode (classifier evaluation breaking down on OOD attribute combinations like bearded females) rather than a generic disclaimer.
Reasonably transparent reproducibility statement with detailed implementation configurations (Table 5) and promise to release code.
weaknesses: The causal mechanism modeling (Eqn. 2-3) assumes a known ground-truth causal graph is provided a priori; the paper does not address causal discovery or robustness to a misspecified/incorrect graph, which limits applicability to settings where the causal structure is uncertain — this is a common limitation in the field but is not discussed as a limitation in the paper.

Comparisons in the main tables (Tables 1-4) are against relatively dated baselines (CausalVAE 2021, DisDiffAE 2022, CausalDiffAE 2024, VAE/HVAE/GAN) rather than the more recent and closely related diffusion-based counterfactual methods explicitly discussed in related work (e.g., Rasal et al. 2025 semantic abduction, Xia et al. 2025 decoupled CFG, Pan & Bareinboim 2024), making it harder to assess whether the reported gains hold against the strongest current competitors.

The 'up to X% reduction' framing in the abstract and contributions (e.g., 91% MAE reduction, 87% FID reduction, 50% MAE reduction, 81% FID reduction — inconsistent figures appear between abstract and contributions bullet list) selectively highlights best-case numbers rather than reporting aggregate/average improvements, and some interventions show clearly worse performance than baselines (e.g., Table 2 do(br) and do(bl) F1 for 'Ours' are sometimes lower than HVAE), which is not transparently reconciled in the main text discussion.

The attention-guidance (AG) module, while presented as optional, is inconsistently helpful (Appendix D.3 shows it can hurt effectiveness for the plain adapter and only modestly help the full model), and its necessity/generality across domains beyond CelebA is not deeply analyzed, slightly muddying the paper's core contribution claims.

No human perceptual study or clinical validation is included for the medical (ADNI) counterfactuals, despite motivating the work partly with clinical interpretability use cases; automated metrics like FID/CLD may not fully capture anatomical plausibility of MRI edits.

The paper relies on a single Stable Diffusion backbone (SD v1.5) and does not explore scalability to larger/newer T2I backbones or more attributes/deeper causal graphs, leaving open questions about generalization to more complex real-world causal structures with more than ~6 variables.

strengths: The paper provides an unusually thorough motivational study (Appendix B) that convincingly demonstrates specific failure modes of prompt-based T2I editing methods (NTI, MCPL) for counterfactual generation, including prompt sensitivity and lack of fine-grained numeric control -- this grounds the proposed method's necessity empirically rather than just by assertion.

The method is evaluated across three qualitatively different domains (synthetic Pendulum, CelebA faces, ADNI brain MRI), with consistent reporting of four complementary metrics (effectiveness, composition, realism, minimality), which is a relatively comprehensive evaluation protocol.

Extensive ablations are provided (guidance scale, DDIM steps, attention guidance, PAI/CTC components) with both quantitative tables and qualitative cross-attention visualizations that make a reasonably legible case for what each regularizer contributes.

The adapter-based design (freezing the SD backbone, training a lightweight side network) is a sensible and practical engineering choice that avoids costly full fine-tuning across datasets, and the abduction-action-prediction procedure is clearly formalized with pseudocode.
The limitations section is honest about a concrete failure case (OOD classifier evaluation for bearded-women counterfactuals), which is a positive sign of self-critical reporting.
weaknesses: The quantitative comparisons omit several directly relevant and recently cited diffusion-based causal counterfactual baselines (Rasal et al. 2025 'semantic abduction', Pan & Bareinboim 2024 'counterfactual image editing', Xia et al. 2025 'decoupled CFG for counterfactual diffusion'); the paper only compares against VAE/HVAE/GAN/CausalVAE/DisDiffAE/CausalDiffAE, which are comparatively weaker or older baselines, making the 'state-of-the-art' claim in the abstract not fully substantiated against the strongest, most relevant prior diffusion-based SCM work.

Several reported numbers directly contradict the 'best performance across most interventions' narrative without adequate discussion -- e.g., in Table 2 the Beard F1 under do(gender) is 74.4 for the proposed method versus 95.9 (VAE), 99.4 (HVAE), and 92.0 (GAN), a large regression that is not analyzed or explained in the text, raising concerns about selective emphasis on favorable results.

The method presupposes a fully known, hand-specified causal graph and attribute set for each dataset; this strong assumption limits generalizability to real-world settings where causal structure is unknown or only partially specified, and the paper does not study robustness to graph misspecification.

Most main-text quantitative tables (CelebA, Pendulum) lack variance/error bars or multiple-seed evaluation (only the ADNI table reports std), making it hard to judge the statistical reliability of the reported improvements, especially for ablations conducted on a reduced 400-sample validation subset.

Evaluation of 'effectiveness' depends entirely on pretrained anti-causal classifiers/regressors, which the authors themselves acknowledge can misjudge valid counterfactuals that are out-of-distribution relative to the classifier's training data (e.g., bearded women); this casts some doubt on the reliability of the primary quantitative metric used throughout the paper, without a clear mitigation or sensitivity analysis.

The causal mechanism modeling itself (additive noise model with MLP, Eq. 2-3) is fairly standard and largely adapted from prior causal representation learning work (e.g., CausalVAE, DeepSCM) rather than being a novel technical contribution; the core novelty is concentrated in the adapter/injection/regularization engineering rather than in causal modeling advances.

Test-time generation requires DDIM inversion of a real input image (not unconditional sampling), and the paper does not thoroughly discuss how inversion error at higher CFG scales interacts with the reported minimality/realism trade-offs beyond a brief ablation, despite this being central to the pipeline's practical reliability.

The paper is dense with many acronyms, multi-panel figures (e.g., Figure 2's six-panel comparison), and cross-referenced appendices, which somewhat hampers self-contained readability of the main text.

strengths: Thorough and well-designed motivational study (Sec 2.2, Appendix B) that clearly diagnoses two concrete failure modes of existing T2I-based editing (prompt sensitivity/instability and attribute entanglement) before motivating the proposed architecture — this grounds the method in empirical evidence rather than assumption.

The core idea of keeping the diffusion backbone frozen and injecting causal structure via a lightweight adapter plus prompt-aligned token embeddings is a sensible, scalable combination of controllable-diffusion (ControlNet/T2I-Adapter-style) techniques with explicit SCM-based causal mechanisms, avoiding costly full fine-tuning across datasets.

Extensive empirical evaluation spanning three very different domains (synthetic Pendulum, CelebA faces, ADNI brain MRI) and four complementary metrics (effectiveness, composition, realism, minimality), with generally strong and sometimes large improvements (e.g., FID and LPIPS reductions on CelebA, MAE reductions on Pendulum/ADNI).

Detailed ablations isolating the contribution of PAI and CTC regularizers, supported by qualitative cross-attention visualizations (Fig. 3c, Fig. 8c, Appendix D/E) that convincingly show improved semantic-spatial alignment and reduced spurious correlation (e.g., bearded-female example).

Good reproducibility practices: detailed algorithm boxes (Alg. 1–4), hyperparameter tables per dataset, metric definitions, and an honest limitations section describing evaluation pitfalls from OOD counterfactuals (e.g., bearded-female misclassification) rather than hiding them.

Additional robustness analyses (guidance scale, DDIM steps, attention guidance) in the appendix show the authors probed sensitivity of their design choices rather than reporting only a single cherry-picked configuration.
weaknesses: The main quantitative comparisons (Tables 1–4) are against relatively dated baselines (VAE, HVAE, GAN, CausalVAE, DisDiffAE, CausalDiffAE); more recent diffusion-based causal counterfactual methods explicitly discussed in related work (e.g., Rasal et al. 2025 semantic abduction, Xia et al. 2025 decoupled CFG) are not included as quantitative baselines, leaving the paper's claim of 'state-of-the-art' only partially substantiated against the strongest contemporary competitors.

Results are mixed in several places: e.g., Table 2 shows the proposed method underperforming HVAE on some do(a)/do(br) F1 scores, and Table 1 shows CausalDiffAE beating the proposed method on shadow-length MAE under several interventions, which somewhat undercuts the 'state-of-the-art across most attributes' framing.

The optional Attention Guidance (AG) module shows inconsistent benefits — it sometimes reduces intervention effectiveness substantially (e.g., Age F1 drop from 38.2 to 28.1 for the plain adapter in Table 8), indicating the auxiliary component is not robustly beneficial and its interaction with the core regularizers is not fully explained.

The method presupposes a known, hand-specified causal graph and attribute set for each domain; there is no study of robustness to graph misspecification or of automatic causal discovery, which limits applicability to settings where the causal structure is uncertain or contested (a common situation in many real-world domains beyond CelebA/ADNI/Pendulum).

Evaluation relies entirely on automatic metrics (FID, LPIPS, CLD, classifier F1/MAE) without any human perceptual study, despite the paper's central claims being about faithful, identity-preserving, human/clinically interpretable counterfactuals — this is a meaningful gap for claims about visual fidelity and identity preservation.

Most result tables (Pendulum, CelebA) do not report variance/standard deviation or significance across seeds (only ADNI does), making it hard to assess whether reported improvements are robust versus run-to-run noise, especially given the qualitative/ablation results are based on a reduced validation subset (400 samples) with noted metric shifts.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: the paper conducts a systematic motivational study (Sec 2.2, Appendix B) showing concrete failure modes of existing T2I editing methods (NTI, MCPL) for counterfactual generation—prompt sensitivity, attribute entanglement, and inability to perform fine-grained continuous edits—which convincingly justifies the need for the proposed approach.

Broad and thorough empirical validation across four diverse datasets (synthetic Pendulum, CelebA, CelebA-HQ, ADNI brain MRI) spanning both natural and medical imaging domains, with consistent state-of-the-art or competitive results on effectiveness, composition, realism, and minimality metrics.

Practical and modular design: injecting causal semantics via a lightweight adapter while freezing the backbone avoids expensive retraining, and the method is shown to generalize to a different backbone family (SD3/DiT with flow matching and FlowEdit), supporting claims of scalability and generality.

Extensive ablation and sensitivity analyses (guidance scale, DDIM steps, attention guidance, PAI/CTC components) with both quantitative tables and qualitative attention-map visualizations that make the contribution of each component interpretable and well supported.

Transparent discussion of limitations, including an explicit appendix on counterfactual identifiability caveats (DDIM inversion is only approximate) and an appendix exploring relaxation of the known-causal-graph assumption via differentiable causal discovery, showing the authors did not oversell theoretical guarantees.
weaknesses: Technical novelty is somewhat incremental: the core contributions (adapter/ControlNet-style side network, prompt-aligned token injection, and InfoNCE-style contrastive disentanglement) are largely recombinations of existing techniques (T2I-Adapter/ControlNet, textual inversion, contrastive learning) applied to the counterfactual setting, rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

The causal mechanism itself is a simple MLP/normalizing-flow additive noise model reused from prior benchmarks; the paper's main innovation is in how attributes are injected into the diffusion backbone rather than in causal modeling per se, which somewhat narrows the causal-inference contribution.

Evaluation of 'effectiveness' and some other metrics relies on classifiers/regressors trained on the same attribute distributions used for generation, raising some concern about circularity; there is no independent (e.g., human or clinical expert) validation of the medical image counterfactuals' plausibility despite the emphasis on clinical relevance.

Reported headline statistics (e.g., '91% MAE reduction on Pendulum', '87% FID reduction on ADNI' in the abstract vs. different numbers such as '50% MAE reduction on ADNI', '81% FID reduction on CelebA' in the intro) appear to be selectively drawn from different specific attributes/interventions across tables, which could give an overly favorable impression if not read carefully against the detailed per-attribute tables.

The minimality metric (CLD) shows only marginal gains over baselines in several tables (e.g., ADNI CLD 0.346 vs 0.347 HVAE, CelebA CLD 0.310 vs 0.299 VAE), and attention guidance—positioned as a key tool for localized editing—sometimes reduces intervention effectiveness (Table 8), indicating the effectiveness/identity-preservation trade-off is not fully resolved.

Formal counterfactual identifiability is not established; the reversibility analysis is an empirical proxy rather than a guarantee, which somewhat tempers the strength of the 'faithful counterfactual generation' claim in the title/abstract.

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation spanning four diverse datasets (synthetic Pendulum, CelebA, CelebA-HQ, ADNI brain MRI), covering both face attributes and medical imaging domains.

A clear and well-motivated empirical study (Appendix B) convincingly demonstrates the weaknesses of pure prompt-based T2I editing methods (NTI, MCPL) for counterfactual generation, which motivates the proposed design.

The adapter-based design is lightweight and reuses a frozen diffusion backbone, avoiding full fine-tuning, and the authors show transferability to a different backbone (SD3/DiT via FlowEdit), suggesting reasonable architectural generality.

Extensive ablations (guidance scale, DDIM steps, attention guidance, PAI/CTC components) and qualitative visualizations (cross-attention maps) are provided, giving some insight into how each regularizer affects disentanglement.

The paper is transparent about limitations such as the known-causal-graph assumption and lack of formal counterfactual identifiability guarantees (Appendix F, G), and includes a preliminary extension toward causal discovery.
weaknesses: The central claim of 'faithful counterfactual generation' rests on the strong assumption of a known, correct causal graph and ground-truth attribute labels for every target domain; the causal mechanism itself is only a shallow additive-noise MLP per node, which is a fairly standard/simple structural model rather than a novel causal contribution. The attempt to relax this assumption (Appendix G) is explicitly described as preliminary and the paper admits full graph recovery from observational data 'remains fundamentally challenging,' undermining the paper's core motivation of causal faithfulness in realistic (graph-unknown) settings.

Reported gains are inconsistent and sometimes cherry-picked: in Table 1, CausalDiffAE still outperforms Causal-Adapter on several shadow-length/position metrics; in Table 2, HVAE actually beats the proposed method on Age and Bald F1, and the CLD (minimality) metric for 'Ours' (0.310) is actually *worse* than VAE (0.299) and GAN comparisons, contradicting the claimed 'faithful' and 'minimal' editing narrative highlighted in the abstract (e.g., '91% MAE reduction,' '87% FID reduction' are best-case numbers not representative of the overall trend).

No formal theoretical guarantee of counterfactual identifiability is provided; the paper's own Appendix F concedes that DDIM-inversion-based abduction is only approximately valid and that 'exact theoretical identifiability remains an open challenge,' which weakens the soundness of the causal claims central to the paper's title and abstract.

Baseline comparisons for VAE/HVAE/GAN in main tables appear to be single-run numbers taken from prior work without variance, while the proposed method reports means over seeds only in the appendix; this makes head-to-head statistical significance unclear, especially given the generally small differences in several key metrics (e.g., CLD across methods differs by only ~0.01).

Ablation and sensitivity analyses (guidance scale, DDIM steps, attention guidance) are conducted on only 400 validation samples, a small and potentially noisy subset for comparing FID/CLD differences that are themselves often marginal.

The approach fundamentally requires a fixed, enumerable set of semantic attributes and a textual prompt template per domain; scalability to larger attribute sets, more complex causal graphs, or free-form/continuous relationships beyond simple additive-noise mechanisms is not demonstrated, limiting the generality implied by the 'modular framework' framing.

Evaluation of 'effectiveness' and 'minimality' relies entirely on separately trained classifiers/regressors and an unconditional VAE latent space (CLD), which may be imperfect proxies for true causal faithfulness and could themselves have idiosyncratic biases not controlled for.

The method combines several existing ideas (ControlNet/T2I-adapter-style side branches, textual-inversion-style token learning, InfoNCE contrastive loss, DDIM inversion/attention-guided editing) in a new application context; while the combination is reasonably engineered, the degree of genuine methodological novelty beyond integration of known techniques is modest.

strengths: The paper provides an unusually thorough experimental validation spanning four datasets across different domains (synthetic Pendulum, CelebA, CelebA-HQ, ADNI brain MRI), with consistent and substantial quantitative gains over VAE/GAN/diffusion-autoencoder baselines on effectiveness, composition, realism, and minimality metrics.

The core idea of treating causal semantic attributes as auxiliary control signals injected via a pluggable, frozen-backbone adapter is a practical and scalable alternative to prior methods that require full retraining or per-sample optimization (e.g., NTI, MCPL), and this is well-supported by the motivational study (Appendix B) documenting concrete failure modes of pure prompt-based editing (instability to synonym choice, entanglement, inability to do fine-grained continuous edits).

Extensive and informative ablations are provided (guidance scale, DDIM steps, attention guidance, PAI/CTC components), with both quantitative tables and qualitative cross-attention visualizations (Fig. 9, 15-17) that convincingly show how each regularizer reduces spurious correlations and improves semantic-spatial alignment.
Generalization is demonstrated across two different diffusion backbones (SD1.5 U-Net and SD3 DiT with flow matching/FlowEdit), supporting the claim that the adapter design is backbone-agnostic.

The paper is commendably forthright about its limitations: Appendix F explicitly discusses that strong empirical reversibility does not constitute a formal identifiability guarantee, and Appendix G acknowledges and empirically probes the known-causal-graph assumption via a causal discovery extension, rather than hiding these issues.
weaknesses: The method fundamentally depends on a predefined, correct causal graph over semantic attributes; while this is common in the field and the authors provide a discovery-based mitigation (Appendix G), the mitigation study itself shows that graph recovery from purely observational data is unreliable, meaning the core claim of 'faithful counterfactual generation' is contingent on an assumption that is hard to satisfy in real applications without the predefined graph.

Statistical rigor is uneven: most headline results (Tables 1-4, 6-9, 13) are reported as single numbers without variance across seeds, while only a couple of tables (e.g., Table 12) report standard deviations over three seeds; given the many close comparisons (e.g., CelebA-HQ smiling F1: 94.15 vs 94.93 for DiffCounter), it is unclear whether reported improvements are significant.

Some baseline results used for comparison (e.g., VCI F1=3.39 for eyeglasses in Table 4, or various GAN/VAE CelebA numbers) are taken from prior reported benchmarks rather than reproduced under identical conditions, raising concerns about comparability and whether baselines were given a fair/matched evaluation protocol.

The qualitative findings in the motivational study (Fig. 10, Appendix B) rely on subjective human judgment of edit success/failure with no inter-rater agreement or quantitative criterion reported, weakening the evidentiary strength of the claimed systematic limitations of NTI/MCPL.

Attention Guidance, while beneficial for realism/FID, is shown to sometimes reduce intervention effectiveness (Table 8), and its benefit is inconsistent across adapter variants (helps regularized variants, hurts the plain adapter) — this trade-off is somewhat glossed over in the main text, which frames AG primarily as a positive addition.

The causal mechanism model itself (additive noise MLP, or normalizing flow borrowed from the benchmark) is fairly simple, and the main technical novelty is the combination of adapter-based conditioning with prompt-aligned token injection and a token-contrastive loss — effective, but an incremental combination of existing ideas (ControlNet-style adapters, textual inversion, InfoNCE) rather than a conceptually new causal generative mechanism.

Medical image resolution is modest (ADNI processed at 192x192 downsampled to 64x64 for training), which may limit the practical utility of the claimed fine-grained anatomical control in real clinical settings despite the strong FID/MAE numbers reported.
